newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky opposes working with Austria's far right.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky opposes working with Austria's far right.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky quashed dissenting voices in his Social Democratic Party on Monday when he ruled out any move to cosy up to a far right buoyed by success in European Parliament elections in October.

The Social Democrats, in power in Austria alone or in coalition since 1945, slumped to an all-time low in the Eeuropean Union's parliamentary elections, securing just 60,000 votes more than Joerg Haider's far right Freedom Party (FPOe).

Some Social Democrats, among them senior figures, called for changes to the party leadership after the October 13 poll, with others urging the party to reconsider an outright ban on working with the far right.

"The SPOe (Social Democratic Party) remains firm to the principles of democracy, social justice and anti-fascism and will not entertain any cooperation with the FPOe of Joerg Haider," Vranitzky told a news conference.
The chancellor said that his party's decision-making committee had discussed reviewing its policy towards the far right but had opposed any change.
"The committee underlined there cannot be any cooperation with Haider's FPOe because there are doubts about its commitment to fundamental principles of democracy," he said.

The fact that the centre-left Social Democrats even considered any future cooperation with the nationalist far right on a federal government level was a mark of the jitters running through the SPOe following the Euro-poll.
The Social Democrats took 29.2 percent of the vote, compared to the 38 percent it won in a general election in December 1995.
Haider's support rose to 27.6 percent, gaining votes from Austrians disenchanted with their country's recently acquired EU membership and an economic slowdown.

The conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, which won 29.5 percent of votes in the Euro-election, have ruled in coalition with Vranitzky for nearly 11 years but the partnership is at best uneasy.
The coalition government collapsed in October last year in a budget row, forcing the December snap election.

Political research analysts have warned that the Social Democrats should heed concerns of its traditional working class supporters, who have linked two years of EU membership with rising unemployment, factory closures and company takeovers.
Haider based his Euro-campaign on opposing the Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union and a single currency, winning around 50 percent of the blue collar vote.
An opinion poll in the respected Standard newspaper on Monday gave Vranitzky more to worry about.

The Linz-based research institute Market said 52 percent of men and 60 percent of women agreed new policy ideas were needed from the government. A total of 52 percent said they were dissatisfied with the direction in which Austria was moving.
